text: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets a, b, c, with distinct indices, that sum to zero. The result must not contain duplicate triplets.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. So I list every triple that sums to zero, but deduplicated by value — minus one, zero, one should appear once even if the array has repeats. For minus one, zero, one, two, minus one, minus four, the answer is minus one, minus one, two, and minus one, zero, one. Does order within a triplet or across triplets matter?
No, any order is fine. n is up to three thousand, and values are between minus ten to the fifth and ten to the fifth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would use three nested loops — n cubed is two point seven times ten to the tenth here, way too slow, plus messy dedup. This problem reminds me of fixing one value and running a sorted two-pointer pair search on the rest. Fix the anchor, nums of i, and the rest becomes: find two numbers summing to minus nums of i. If I sort first, that inner search is a converging two-pointer scan in linear time, and sorting also makes dedup simple, since equal values become adjacent. Total: quadratic time, constant extra space beyond the output.
Dedup is the tricky part. Walk me through where duplicates can arise.

Three spots, all skip adjacent equal values, thanks to sorting. One: the outer anchor — if nums of i equals nums of i minus one, the same anchor would reproduce the same triplets, so I continue. Two and three: after recording a hit, I move l up and r down, then skip any l whose value equals nums of l minus one, and any r whose value equals nums of r plus one — the same left or right value as the triplet I just took.

Here's the plan. One: sort, and for each anchor i, skip it if it repeats the previous value. Two: set l to i plus one and r to n minus one, and move by the sign of the three-number sum. Three: on zero, record it, advance both, then skip duplicate l and r values. I compare against nums of l minus one and nums of r plus one because I advance before skipping. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I sort, then loop over anchors, skipping a repeated anchor. Inside, l and r converge: a negative sum moves l up, a positive sum moves r down, and a zero sum gets pushed into the answer. One thing worth flagging — the hit branch. I do l plus plus and r minus minus first, and only then skip repeats, comparing each pointer to the neighbor it just left. Both skip loops also check l less than r, so they can't run past each other or off the array.

Let's dry-run the code. Minus one, zero, one, two, minus one, minus four sorts to minus four, minus one, minus one, zero, one, two — expected two triplets. The anchor that matters is the first minus one: the pair search takes minus one, minus one, two, then moves inward and takes minus one, zero, one. The second minus one is skipped as a duplicate anchor, so nothing repeats. Both triplets found once. That matches. And for four zeros: after the first hit, l and r meet, and the outer dedup skips the other zeros, so just zero, zero, zero.

Yes — once nums of i is above zero, every later element is positive too, so no triple can sum to zero, and I could break. My code doesn't include that check; it's only a constant-factor win. The worst case, with many negatives and zeros, stays quadratic.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is quadratic: the n log n sort is absorbed, and it's n anchors times a linear converge. Space is constant extra beyond the output, apart from the sort's own stack, which is logarithmic. Oh, one more thing — this generalizes. The four-number version wraps one more fixed loop, so cubic time; the general k-number version is a recursion whose base case is exactly this two-pointer pair search. And the closest-sum variant reuses the same converge, but tracks the best distance instead of deduplicating.
Solid — the reframing to a sorted pair search, all three dedup points, and the k-number generalization. That's everything I wanted.
